title: ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists' signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons
titleZh: ChatGPT 正在将真正的漫画家的签名添加到假《纽约客》漫画中
author: rdmuser
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: At the pearly gates, Dolly Parton, in a sparkling gown, stands arm in arm with Tim Curry, dressed as Dr. Frank-N-Furter. “I knew I chose the right plus one,” Parton says to God, who is standing at heaven’s reception desk.

That’s the premise of a cartoon that went viral on Twitter in the days after the legendary entertainers’ deaths in late August. One tweet of the cartoon received 25,000 likes, while other versions of the image circulated on Facebook, Instagram, and Bluesky. In the bottom right corner of the cartoon is the pen name “BLOPER,” the signature of New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper. But Loper didn’t draw the cartoon, or sign it. It was generated by ChatGPT and first posted to Facebook by a Dolly Parton fan. In the comments section of her post, she wrote she had simply asked ChatGPT to make “a New Yorker-style cartoon.” “I had people writing to me about this cartoon, asking if it was mine,” Loper told me. First came a text from his twin brother, whose friend had seen the AI-generated image. Emails and DMs on social media from strangers followed. “It was very surreal,” he said.

This wasn’t the first time ChatGPT had reproduced Loper’s signature. In May, a stranger reached out over Instagram to warn Loper that his pen name had appeared in an image output by the chatbot. Over the summer, Loper found additional examples in a Reddit forum about ChatGPT, where users had been posting similar New Yorker-style cartoons they had generated. Loper already knew his work was “out there, getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” he said. But an image generator faking his signature felt more personal. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood.” These days, cartoon signatures are more than a byline. In an era where cartoons are regularly stripped from their original context and circulated on blogs and social media without proper licensing, they can also act as a watermark that ties an illustration to its original creator. “The signature for me is the certificate of authenticity. I only put it on work that I’m putting on the internet that I feel needs to be recognized as from my hand,” Loper told me. “If I put my name on it, it’s official, it’s mine. It really is a brand. It’s the mark that I made.” Loper isn’t the only New Yorker cartoonist whose signature has been reproduced by ChatGPT. In the same online forums are dozens of images with those of other prominent contributors, including Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, Pat Byrnes, Peter Vey, and Jason Adam Katzenstein. In my own tests, ChatGPT output cartoons with signatures of some of the magazine’s most established cartoonists, past and present, including George Booth, Liza Donnelly, Ellis Rosen, and Saul Steinberg. In all, I documented more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists whose signatures have been used by OpenAI’s image generator without permission or compensation. “We believe the future of creativity is one that is fundamentally human, and our focus is on building tools that empower human creativity and creators,” said a spokesperson for OpenAI in a statement. “We very much appreciate the community flagging bugs and unintended behavior by our models, so we can address them.” After I notified OpenAI of the issue, ChatGPT began to output a new message when I asked it to generate New Yorker-style cartoons: “This prompt may violate our guardrails concerning similarity to third-party content.” Still, as of the publication of this story, it continues to sign some of the generic cartoons it generates with the names of real New Yorker cartoonists.

In my tests, ChatGPT regularly generated cartoons with the hallmarks of the 101-year-old magazine’s house style: a black-and-white, single-panel illustration with a sparse background, clean linework, and a sardonic caption — or at least, an approximation of one. Some of ChatGPT’s punch lines don’t make sense. Not every image came with a signature, and some included pen names that were gibberish. But the signatures that did appear were regularly those of real contributors to the magazine, including older cartoonists, like Warren Miller, who published in the 1960s. “I can see the DNA of my work in there, but it still doesn’t look like something I drew,” said Emily Flake, who’s been a New Yorker contributor since 2008. Several ChatGPT-generated cartoons posted online are signed with her pen name, “e. flake.” “It’s kind of like seeing a distant cousin.” The character stances and shading contained echoes of Flake’s visual identity, but she said overall they looked more like amalgamations of several different cartoonists’ illustration styles. Each signature, though, was undeniably hers. “It’s like somebody attributed a quote to me that I didn’t say.” Left: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Emily Flake’s signature that was posted to a Reddit forum in June. Right: A real Emily Flake cartoon published in The New Yorker on August 20, 2026 and licensed via The Cartoon Bank.

Top: A cartoon generated by ChatGPT and signed with Emily Flake’s signature that was posted to a Reddit forum in June. Bottom: A real Emily Flake cartoon published in The New Yorker on August 20, 2026 and licensed via The Cartoon Bank.

comments.author: Isamu
comments.textRawHtml:
The part of the AI generating the mashup doesn’t really understand what the signature means, or how it may be interpreted, it’s just a visual part of a New Yorker cartoon. Elsewhere in ChatGPT there is plenty of information about signatures and what they mean, and what plagiarism is.

It’s not organized like a human brain, it shouldn’t be surprising that unusual results occur. They are approximating human intelligence from a different angle. It’s interesting to see the improvements in areas like this that require introspection that isn’t fully wired up yet.

[edit] I should add that a human making a New Yorker cartoon is extremely iterative and introspective. Current generative AI is meant to push it out, and you can do the iteration and introspection yourself.
comments.textZhHtml:
生成混搭的人工智能部分并不真正理解签名的含义，或者如何解释它，它只是《纽约客》漫画的视觉部分。 ChatGPT 中的其他地方有大量有关签名及其含义以及抄袭是什么的信息。

它的组织方式不像人脑，因此出现异常结果也就不足为奇了。他们从不同的角度接近人类的智力。看到像这样需要内省但尚未完全连接的领域的改进是很有趣的。

[编辑]我应该补充一点，制作《纽约客》卡通片的人是极其迭代和内省的。现在的生成式AI就是推出来的，你可以自己去迭代、反省。

children.author: amelius
children.textRawHtml:
Us: "Hey, AI is using copyrighted works!"

Them: "AI is not a dumb copying machine; it processes the work so it becomes a derived work; it's just like how a human learns things from existing works and produces new, authentic works."

Us: "Hey, AI is copying signatures!"

Them: "You should view AI as a dumb copying machine; AI is not organized like the human brain."
children.textZhHtml:
我们：“嘿，人工智能正在使用受版权保护的作品！”

他们：“人工智能不是一台愚蠢的复印机；它对作品进行处理，使其成为衍生作品；这就像人类如何从现有作品中学习并产生新的、真实的作品。”

我们：“嘿，人工智能正在复制签名！”

他们：“你应该将人工智能视为一台愚蠢的复印机；人工智能的组织方式不像人脑。”

children.author: bonesss
children.textRawHtml:
Kinda like how if I break some plates at a restaurant I have to pay for it, but if Tony Soprano breaks them the restaurant pays him.

Protection is a heck of a business model, if you can get away with it.
children.textZhHtml:
有点像如果我在餐厅打破了一些盘子，我必须为此付费，但如果托尼·索普拉诺打破了它们，餐厅就会付钱给他。

如果你能逃脱惩罚的话，保护是一种很棒的商业模式。

children.author: wholinator2
children.textRawHtml:
Might be an example of the Goomba Fallacy [1]. Though that brings the interesting point of how could you ever know whether the same person/group has contradictory beliefs if you aren't seeing the exact same account posting an example of it. It seems like it could be an easy out to just say "Goomba!" whenever hypocrisy is observed.

[1]: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Goomba_fallacy
children.textZhHtml:
可能是 Goomba 谬误的一个例子 [1]。尽管如此，有趣的是，如果您没有看到完全相同的帐户发布示例，您如何知道同一个人/团体是否具有相互矛盾的信念。看起来只要说“Goomba！”就可以很容易地解决这个问题。每当发现虚伪行为时。

[1]: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Goomba_fallacy

children.author: streetfighter64
children.textRawHtml:
The issue of whether the AI-generated images are copyright infringement is entirely separate from whether the AI is capable of independently creating derived works.

See for example https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VMG_Salsoul_v._Ciccone which decided that it's allowed to sample certain instruments etc. in music production. Could AI be compared to such sampling? Perhaps.

Though, what actually decides isn't really the merits of one's case, but rather who has the money to fight in court. And we all know who'd win in AI companies vs cartoonists, unfortunately.
children.textZhHtml:
AI生成的图像是否侵犯版权的问题与AI是否能够独立创作衍生作品的问题完全分开。

例如https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VMG_Salsoul_v._Ciccone决定允许在音乐制作中采样某些乐器等。人工智能可以与这样的采样进行比较吗？也许吧。

不过，真正决定的并不是案件的是非曲直，而是谁有钱去法庭打架。不幸的是，我们都知道人工智能公司与漫画家谁会获胜。

AI boosters take note: this sort of thing is exactly what skeptics have in mind when they insist that you are nowhere near "AGI" and have not meaningfully passed Turing tests and your claims of goalpost-shifting are fake. You have been aiming at straw goalposts.

> 它的组织方式不像人脑，因此出现不寻常的结果并不奇怪。他们从不同的角度接近人类的智力。看到此类需要内省但尚未完全连接的领域的改进是很有趣的。

人工智能支持者请注意：当怀疑论者坚称你距离“AGI”还很远，还没有有意义地通过图灵测试并且你关于球门柱转移的说法是假的时，这种事情完全就是他们所想到的。你一直瞄准的是稻草球门柱。

children.author: zahlman
children.textRawHtml: Being able to fix the problems doesn't change that the system fundamentally works differently.

children.author: CrazyStat
children.textRawHtml:
A couple weeks ago someone on this website argued that expecting AGI to be able to learn from experience was moving the goalposts.

Turing discussed learning from experience extensively in his classic thinking machines paper.
children.textZhHtml:
几周前，该网站上有人认为，期望 AGI 能够从经验中学习正在改变目标。

图灵在他的经典思维机器论文中广泛讨论了从经验中学习。

children.author: dv_dt
children.textRawHtml: Its a huge stretch saying it's even approximating human intelligence. All llms are lossy, recombinant, compressed search indexes. There is no introspection - and what we mostly see is fairly rudimentary heuristic programming loops wrapped around them - which tells you how powerful a tool llms are, but don't mistake the capabilities of the tool for reasoning in any form.
children.textZhHtml: 说它甚至接近人类智能是一个巨大的延伸。所有 llms 都是有损、重组、压缩的搜索索引。没有内省 - 我们主要看到的是围绕它们的相当基本的启发式编程循环 - 这告诉您 llms 工具有多么强大，但不要误认为该工具的功能用于任何形式的推理。

children.author: viraptor
children.textRawHtml: Have you got a proof that humans are not lossy, recombinant, compressed search indexes as well? Because that whole claim depends on it and we don't really know that much about that human brains really are.
children.textZhHtml: 你有证据证明人类也不是有损、重组、压缩的搜索索引吗？因为整个主张都取决于它，而我们对人类大脑的真正了解并不多。

children.author: JohnMakin
children.textRawHtml:
The burden of proof does not lie there, this is a popular fallacy people love to reflexively respond with.

If you don't know that much about human brains, then how on earth can you make the claim that these possess human intelligence? The burden of proof doesn't lie on the "prove it's NOT as intelligent as a human" side.

Thinking about this for 5 seconds reveals how silly this line of thinking is, sorry, and this exact comment is made 500 times a day here.
children.textZhHtml:
举证责任不在于那里，这是人们喜欢条件反射地回应的一个流行谬论。

如果你对人类大脑了解不多，那么你到底怎么能声称它们拥有人类智能呢？举证责任并不在于“证明它不像人类那么聪明”。

思考这个问题 5 秒钟就会发现这种想法是多么愚蠢，抱歉，这个确切的评论在这里每天被提出 500 次。

children.author: viraptor
children.textRawHtml:
> then how on earth can you make the claim that these possess human intelligence?

I'm not making any such claim. It's not some black and white situation where you automatically take the extreme opposing side if you raise an issue with some take.

> The burden of proof doesn't lie on the "prove it's NOT as intelligent as a human" side.

It's on the side making any specific claim.
children.textZhHtml:
> 那么你到底怎么能声称它们拥有人类智能呢？

我不会做出任何这样的声明。这并不是某种黑白分明的情况，如果你提出了一些观点的问题，你就会自动采取极端的对立面。

>举证责任并不在于“证明它不如人类聪明”的一方。

而是在提出任何具体主张的一方。
